title: Gobind is everything
hookLine: sabh gobind hai: everything is Gobind; there is nothing without Him (Asa, Namdev, ang 485)

cards: Snap the cord of a necklace and you learn something fast. The beads go everywhere: under the couch, into the rug, one rolling off toward the door. While the cord held, you barely noticed it.
You were looking at the beads. Namdev, the printer who sang his way into the Guru Granth Sahib, reached for exactly that picture. Where, in the whole world, is the Lord not?
His answer, in the original, is short. Everything is Gobind.

teach.b: The hymn is in Raag Asa, on Ang 485, and its refrain is sabh gobind hai, sabh gobind hai, gobind bin nahi koi. In paraphrase: everything is Gobind, everything is Gobind; without Gobind there is nothing at all.
Gobind is one of the names for the Lord in the Granth. Namdev gives two pictures.

teach.h: ONE THREAD THROUGH ALL THE BEADS.
teach.b: The first is the necklace: as one thread runs through countless beads, so the Lord runs through everything, warp and weft. The second is water.
Waves, foam and bubbles are not separate from the water. They rise and fall and look like many things, but they're water all the way through. Then Namdev admits this isn't obvious.

teach.h: ONLY A RARE ONE SEES IT.
teach.b: In the same hymn he says the world's dazzling pictures keep people bewildered, and only a rare one understands. That's honest. On plenty of days we see beads, not thread, waves, not water.

So what does he do? He says the Guru's teaching woke his mind, and he invites the listener: look at the Lord's creation, and think it over in your heart. In every heart, within all, there is only the One.
Namdev isn't asking us to pretend the beads aren't there. The colors, the people, the dishes in the sink all stay. He's asking us to notice the thread through them.
Sikhs sing this hymn as gurbani, and its whole teaching fits on one line.

how: Namdev's hymn with the refrain sabh gobind hai is sung in kirtan as gurbani, and Sikhs draw on it to speak of the One present in every heart and all of creation.

o: the teacher who first taught Namdev to sing hymns
the string of beads used to count prayers
a name for the Lord, the one thread through all

games.q: inside the hymn — tap the pairs.

s: Namdev says the world's things aren't really there
he asks us to think it over in the heart and see the One in all, not to deny the beads.
Namdev uses the picture of waves and foam
waves, foam and bubbles are not separate from the water.

games.q: you're Namdev, trying to show how the One can be in so many different things. which picture do you reach for?
o: a king and his many soldiers.
one thread running through countless beads.
a mountain seen from far away.
games.why: the thread through the beads, warp and weft, and then water in every wave, foam and bubble.

practice: Let your eyes land on one thing nearby, a cup, a window, your own hand, rest there a few breaths, and say inside, sabh gobind hai.

Then a second thing, farther away, and a third, a sound, a person or the air itself, letting Namdev's line be the thread through all three. Don't force a feeling; if you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Gobind. One of the names for the Lord in the Granth: the thread through every bead, the water in every wave, Namdev's refrain sabh gobind hai.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Gobind, a name for the Lord in Namdev's refrain sabh gobind hai.

carryVoice: Your line: everything is gobind. The thread is there even on the days you only see beads. Day seven hundred seventy-one.
